translation: Perhaps because Miho and Satsuki see each other so frequently, their expressions and manner of speaking are strikingly similar.
Particularly, the way they eat sweets is so alike; both break cookies into small pieces with their manicured hands before bringing them to their mouth.
I try to remember if they were always like this, but my memory is fuzzy.
I wonder if all the tiny habits and gestures from the last time we met have somehow slipped away from me.
Miho is now married and she bought a used single-family home in her hometown, where friends often gather.

Sometimes she dreads going to her part-time job the next day, but it's her only connection to the world outside the convenience store, and a precious opportunity to interact with other "normal women in their thirties", so she tries to accept Miho's invitations whenever possible.
Today too, it was me along with Miho, Yukari who still has small children, and Satsuki who is also married but doesn't yet have kids.
We all brought cakes over to Miho's house for tea.
That was the first time I felt I had become a part of the world.
It was as if I had been born anew.
On that day, I truly emerged as a normal part of this world.
For the two weeks leading up to the opening, endless practice continued, as we formed pairs or served our fellow employees, treating them as imaginary customers.

Smiling and bowing while looking into the "customer's" eyes, placing sanitary products in paper bags, separating hot items from cold ones in their packaging and disinfecting hands with alcohol when asked for fast food.
There was real money in the cash register to get us used to handling it, but our receipts had "Training" prominently printed on them.
Our counterparts were part-time co-workers wearing the same uniform and somehow this whole thing felt like playing a make-believe shopping game.
My younger sister, two years my junior, was unlike me, a "normal" child.
However, she never shied away from me; rather, she seemed to adore me.
Whenever she got scolded by our mother for some ordinary mischief and I would approach our mother to ask, "Why are you angry?"
Once my question ended the lecture our mum was giving her, my sister always said "Thank you" to me—perhaps feeling that I had shielded her.
I frequently gave away candies and toys which did not interest me much to my little sister.
That's why she was always following me around.
"Dad loved yakitori, so let's roast this and eat it today," I repeated clearly, thinking she hadn't heard me the first time.
My mother looked shocked.
The mom next to her who had brought another child also seemed startled as she opened her eyes, nostrils, and mouth all at once.
Her funny face almost made me laugh; but then I saw her looking at what was in my hand.
That's when it occurred to me that one bird wouldn't be enough.
"Should I catch more?"
When I glanced fleetingly at two or three sparrows walking nearby, my mother finally snapped back to reality—a sharp
"Keiko!" rang out like a desperate accusation.
I quickly bagged a can of coffee, some cigarettes and an American-style hot dog into a small-sized bag.
Meanwhile, the man who had been jingling change in his pocket suddenly reached into his breast pocket as though he just remembered something.
From this gesture, I instantly discerned that he was going to pay with electronic money.
"Welcome, good morning!"
With a slight nod, I accept the can of coffee offered by the male customer.
"Ahand number 5 cigarettes please.
"Certainly," I quickly pull out a Marlboro Light Menthols and scan it at the register.
"Please touch for age confirmation.
As he touches the screen, his glance shifts subtly to the food display case with fast food lined up.
Seeing this, I stop my movement of hand.
When it seems as if the customer is debating whether or not to purchase something else, I decide to stay back and wait before offering to help further by asking "Would you like anything else?".
At the faint sound of jingling coins, I turn around, directing my gaze towards the cash register.
Those who jingle money in their hands or pockets are often people buying cigarettes or newspapers in haste, so I've become sensitive to the sound of money.
Sure enough, there was a man making his way towards the cash register with a canned coffee in one hand whilst burrowing his other hand into his pocket.
With swift movements, I navigated through the store to slip behind the counter so as not to keep this customer waiting.
A convenience store is filled with sounds.
The chime of entering customers, the voice of an idol advertising new products through in-store radio broadcasts.
The shouts of employees, the sound of scanning barcodes.
The sound of items being put in baskets, bags of bread being grabbed, and the noise from heels walking around inside the store.
Everything mixes together to form "the soundscape of a convenience store", constantly touching my eardrums.
